newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr firmer in Tokyo after sleepy Christmas trade.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firmer in Tokyo after sleepy Christmas trade.

text.p: The dollar was a bit firmer in late Tokyo on Wednesday, but its moves were stuck within narrow ranges amid limited participation with most overseas markets closed for Christmas, dealers said.
Commercial purchases and light speculative buying lifted the dollar earlier, but Japanese exporter sales above 114.50 yen inhibited further gains into the 115 yen level, they said.
Activity was concentrated in the morning, as trading became motionless in the afternoon ahead of Christmas holidays in many overseas markets.
"There was commercial buying at the local fixing (at 0100 GMT) and then exporter sales kicked in. That's about all that happened today," said a dealer with a trust bank.

He added that although the greenback managed to overcome sales and rise above an initial resistance of 114.50 yen, 115 yen was still no easy target in the near term given exporters' interest in selling. "Exporters seem content if they can sell at 115 yen," he said.
Opinions were divided over the direction of the dollar after the Christmas holidays.
"I think that the dollar could start rising toward 116 or 117 yen by early next year since factors for dollar buying are outpacing those for selling," said a European bank dealer.

The dollar surged against the Swiss franc in New York on Tuesday to 1.3465 francs, its highest level in nearly 28 months. The franc is likely to be hit further by the sluggish economic growth and low interest rates there, dealers said.
"Like the Swiss franc, the yen with its low interest rates is going to be sold against the dollar," said another dealer.
Dealers also said frail Japanese stock prices would also work to push up the dollar.
Tokyo stocks recovered sharply on Wednesday, with the benchmark Nikkei 225 average closing up 387.70 points or 2.02 percent at 19,549.41.
But dealers said the recovery was far from convincing and added that the stock market could remain vulnerable on the back of a gloomy outlook for Japan's economy next year.
Weak share prices are expected to force the Bank of Japan to maintain its current monetary policy and lead Japanese investors to buy foreign securities with higher returns.

"Japanese pension funds are still seen interested in investing in foreign securities. That's another reason why you should be long on the dollar," said a dealer with a British bank in Tokyo. -- George Nishiyama, Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3-5473-3710
